result: Doves exhibit a pronounced mid-downstroke dip in angle of attack (30.5° ± 3.1° at 27.7% of stroke) that coincides with a peak in power factor and results in reduced aerodynamic drag and peak net aerodynamic force generation. This angle of attack pattern is especially pronounced compared to other species.
evaluation: All three reviewers affirm the findings without questioning the angle of attack measurements or their aerodynamic consequences. Reviewer 1 states 'the evidence for the findings is compelling,' Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'achieve their aims' and 'conclusions...address the intended research aim,' and Reviewer 3 confirms 'the authors achieved their goal' with 'thorough analysis which supports the conclusions convincingly.'

result: The aerodynamic power dip allows excess pectoralis power to be transferred into tensioning the supracoracoideus tendon during downstroke, which can assist the upstroke and improve pectoralis work loop efficiency. A 24.9% ± 17.5% increase in pectoralis power would enable full upstroke powering via elastic storage, and optimal storage timing (31% of stroke) with >35% energy storage achieves work loop shape factors >0.72 ± 0.11 (maximum 0.73 ± 0.10).
evaluation: Reviewers accept the elastic energy storage mechanism and work loop efficiency findings. Reviewer 1 describes the evidence as 'compelling,' Reviewer 2 acknowledges the model 'seems to be quite good at predicting muscle function' and notes the authors 'effectively integrate methods,' and Reviewer 3 states the analysis 'supports the conclusions convincingly' regarding 'the interplay of the pectoralis and supracoracoideus muscles.'

result: Aerodynamic power dominates during downstroke while inertial power dominates upstroke in doves. Inertial power smooths the two peaks in aerodynamic power adjacent to the mid-downstroke dip, reducing the difference from 206.1 ± 248.3 W/kg to 43.0 ± 283.4 W/kg.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question the power partitioning findings. Reviewer 2 notes the model allows 'estimations of muscle function that are not feasible to measure in live birds during flight' and that conclusions 'address the intended research aim,' while Reviewer 3 confirms the 'thorough analysis' supports conclusions about muscle function.

result: Scaling analysis shows that birds with faster wingtip speed need proportionally more pectoralis power, and birds with disproportionally larger wing inertia need to activate the pectoralis earlier to tune their downstroke.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the comparative scaling predictions. Reviewer 2 states the work 'provides predictions for muscle function that can be tested empirically' and has 'implications for biologists studying movement and muscle function more generally,' while Reviewer 3 notes the integration of 'other bird species...into the model for a comparative investigation' was successful.

result: The more rectangular work loops from the current study (shape factor 0.73 ± 0.10) suggest improved work generation compared to triangular work loops from prior strain-gauge measurements (shape factor 0.62).
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the work loop shape comparisons. Reviewer 1 notes the methods combine 'new methods for measuring wing shape and force production combined with previously validated methods in muscle physiology,' and Reviewer 2 acknowledges the model's ability to make 'accurate predictions' about muscle function.

result: The current study calculated average net pectoralis power of 182 ± 48 W/kg (no storage) to 232 ± 60 W/kg (full storage) for doves at 1.23 ± 0.13 m/s, suggesting Tobalske et al. 2003 underestimated power by 1.6% ± 26.6% to 29.4% ± 33.3%.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the power estimates and comparison to prior work. Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'acknowledge and justify their assumptions at each step' and the model 'seems to be quite good at predicting muscle function,' while Reviewer 3 confirms the analysis 'supports the conclusions convincingly.'

result: Hummingbirds show similar aerodynamic power during upstroke and downstroke with inertial power dominant throughout the stroke (likely due to higher wingbeat frequency of 79 Hz vs. 9.8 Hz in doves), and have more similar pectoralis to supracoracoideus mass ratios (2:1 vs. 4.60 ± 0.93 in doves) because they need more upstroke muscle power.
evaluation: Reviewers do not question the hummingbird comparison. Reviewer 3 specifically notes 'other bird species were integrated into the model for a comparative investigation' successfully, and Reviewer 2 acknowledges the work has 'implications for biologists studying movement and muscle function more generally.'

result: Doves primarily use lift for weight support (66.17% ± 10.81% vertical force) with drag contributing secondarily (22.11% ± 4.62%), while during upstroke the folded wings produce minimal aerodynamic force (11.28% ± 2.81% vertical, 2.68% ± 1.49% horizontal).
evaluation: Reviewers accept the aerodynamic force decomposition findings. Reviewer 1 describes evidence as 'compelling' and derived from 'new methods for measuring wing shape and force production,' while Reviewer 3 notes the 'simultaneous application of four high-speed techniques' provides convincing support.

result: The computed pectoralis pull angle for doves in slow flight is lower than chukars during wing-assisted incline running, but would increase toward chukar values if pectoralis moment tensions the supracoracoideus tendon during the second half of downstroke.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the pull angle analysis or predictions. Reviewer 2 notes the work 'provides predictions for muscle function that can be tested empirically,' and Reviewer 3 confirms the analysis 'supports the conclusions convincingly.'

result: Comparative analysis shows the dove's mid-downstroke angle of attack (30.5° ± 3.1°) is especially pronounced compared to Pacific parrotlets (45-60°), barn owls (~30° at higher speeds), hovering hummingbirds (36.9° ± 4.9°), and hovering bats (52.2° ± 5.0°), with bat angle of attack patterns more similar to doves than hummingbirds.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the cross-species comparisons without objection. Reviewer 3 notes the successful 'integration' of other species into the model, and Reviewer 2 acknowledges the broader implications for 'biologists studying movement and muscle function more generally.'
